title: Global Transpiration Changes and Its Drivers in the Future
content:
Abstract

Plant transpiration (E t ), the dominant element of evapotranspiration, plays an important role in hydrological, ecological, and climate processes. However, attributing projected future E t change to elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration ([CO2]), air temperature (T a ), and leaf area index (LAI) remains challenging because these drivers exert opposing and interacting influences. Here, we develop a quantitative first-order attribution framework that combines grid-cell-level sensitivities diagnosed from CMIP6 single-forcing experiments with projected driver changes under Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). Our results show that simulated future global E t shifts from +10.42 ± 11.84 mm yr−1 (+3.9%) under SSP1-2.6 to −14.33 ± 29.91 mm yr−1 (−5.4%) under SSP5-8.5, largely because the diagnosed negative physiological contribution of elevated [CO2] increasingly exceeds the positive contributions associated with increasing T a and LAI under stronger forcing. Spatially, the [CO2]-related reduction is widespread, whereas the T a -related contribution is more pronounced in humid regions and the LAI-related contribution is larger in arid and semi-arid regions. Inter-model spread in the attributed contributions arises substantially from differences in diagnosed sensitivities of ΔE t to changes in [CO2], T a , and LAI, with the LAI-related term showing the largest spread among the three first-order terms considered. These results provide a consistent quantitative basis for interpreting how elevated [CO2], warming, and vegetation dynamics jointly shape projected E t and highlight the need to better represent plant physiological responses, vegetation structural dynamics, and land-atmosphere coupling in Earth System Models.
